units.translation: 10 Etymologicum Magnum 368, 45 s.v. ἐπωμαδόν, after quoting lines I 738–741, continues: (ἤιε:) he followed and departed (these words are read after κρουούσῃ, transposed by W). (δὶς τόσση . . . πέτρη:) twice as large followed the lyre of Amphion as it was struck, compared to the one carried by Zethus. For Zethus and Amphion built the walls of Thebes. Apollonius in the Argonautica.

1 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ὀχμάζω: I hold fast from (ἀπὸ in B) ἔχω, ὄχμος (καὶ added in B), ὀχμάζω . . . for example: I 743–746. In ancient times the tunics had the part at the neck (τὸν τράχηλον in A) and the shoulders (τὴν ὤμην in A) open, as also the part at the feet; and they held it together with close-set brooches (W, συνιὸν in A, illegible in B). He says, then, that when the brooches holding the left side of the tunic and those on the left shoulders were raised, the tunic hung loose down to the left breast, so that it was visible. Apollonius.

Mestor and Electryon held the kingship in common. Mestor's daughter was Hippothoe, and by Poseidon she had Pterelaus. Pterelaus' sons were Teleboas and Taphius, from whom the island is named. But according to some, the sons of Teleboas son of Pterelaus were those called Teleboans. They came and demanded from Electryon the property of their grandmother Hippothoe, and when the sons of Electryon opposed them, they were killed by them. So the Teleboans are the Taphians, either because they drove off the cattle from Argos while living far away (tēle), or from Teleboas son of King Pterelaus, whose brother was Taphius, from whom the island is named.
